learn.title: Simple present passive
learn.html:
We use the passive when the action is more important than the person who does it. Often we do not know who does the action, or it is not important. Form: am / is / are + past participle.

ActivePassive
Police officers give fines.Fines are given by police officers.
People do not allow smoking here.Smoking is not allowed here.
Congress makes the laws.Laws are made by Congress.
Do they pay taxes every year?Are taxes paid every year?
  • The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive sentence.
  • Use by + person only when it is useful or surprising: The law is made by Congress.
  • Questions: Where are tickets sold? Negatives: Pets are not allowed.

watch.wrong: The fine is pay at the bank.
watch.right: The fine is paid at the bank.
watch.why: After be, use the past participle: paid.

watch.wrong: Cars is not allowed in the park.
watch.right: Cars are not allowed in the park.
watch.why: Cars is plural, so use are.
In questions, be goes before the subject.

watch.wrong: Fines are pay by the police.
watch.right: Fines are given by the police.
watch.why: Use a past participle (given), and pay does not fit the meaning here.

learn.title: Simple past passive
learn.html:
For past events, we use was / were + past participle. It is very common in history, news and biographies.

ActivePassive
They signed the law in 1964.The law was signed in 1964.
The police arrested many people.Many people were arrested.
Did they give him a prize?Was he given a prize?
They did not allow women to vote.Women were not allowed to vote.
  • was / were born is always passive: She was born in 1990. (not She is born)
  • Regular verbs end in -ed; irregular verbs have a special form: give - gave - given, write - wrote - written.
  • Use by to name who did the action: The speech was heard by thousands of people.

watch.why: After was, use the past participle (given), not the past simple (gave).
Laws is plural, so use were.
Birth is in the past, so use was born.
Passive questions use was / were, not did.

learn.title: both...and, either...or, neither...nor
learn.html:
These pairs join two ideas in one sentence.

PairMeaningExample
both ... andthe two things togetherBoth the judge and the lawyer arrived early.
either ... orone thing or the otherYou can pay either online or at the bank.
neither ... nornot one and not the otherNeither my boss nor I knew the rule.
  • Neither...nor already has a negative meaning. Do not add not.
  • Use the same type of word after each part: either a fine or a warning; neither fair nor legal.
  • With both...and the verb is plural: Both Ana and Luis know the law.

watch.wrong: Neither the manager or the workers knew the rule.
watch.right: Neither the manager nor the workers knew the rule.
watch.why: Neither goes with nor, not with or.

watch.wrong: Neither of them doesn't have a license.
watch.right: Neither of them has a license.
watch.why: Neither is already negative; do not add another negative.

watch.wrong: Both my brother and my sister is lawyers.
watch.right: Both my brother and my sister are lawyers.
watch.why: Both...and joins two people, so the verb is plural.

watch.wrong: You can either pay online and at the bank.
watch.right: You can pay either online or at the bank.
watch.why: Either goes with or, not with and.

learn.title: Useful expressions
learn.html:
• Excuse me, officer. Could you explain the rule, please? — asking an authority politely.
  • I'm sorry. I didn't know it was against the law. — explaining a mistake.
  • How much is the fine, and where can I pay it? — asking about a fine.
  • If it is paid within ten days, there is a discount. — talking about deadlines and conditions.
  • I'd like to make an appointment to talk about my rights. — asking for legal help.
  • I have the right to speak to a lawyer. — saying what your rights are.
  • Please stop. That comment makes me uncomfortable. — asking for respect at work, calmly and clearly.
  • Everyone deserves to be treated with respect. — a general professional statement.

Use the simple past passive at least four times (was born, was taught, was chosen...). Opening: The person I admire most is...

write.model: My grandmother, Rosa Martinez, is the person I admire most. She was born in a small village in Oaxaca in 1948. Her family was very poor, and she was sent to work on a farm when she was ten. She was never allowed to go to school, so her mother taught her to read at night. When she was twenty, she moved to Mexico City, where she was hired as a cleaner in a hospital. She studied in the evenings, and in 1975 she was promoted to nurse's assistant. She worked there for thirty years, and her kindness was known by every patient. Both her children went to university, and she was invited to their graduation. Today she is eighty, and she is still the first person in our family to help anyone in trouble. I admire her because she never gave up.

reading.title: Martin Luther King Jr.: Changing the Law Peacefully
reading.intro: Read about the life of a civil-rights leader and answer.
paragraphs: Martin Luther King Jr. was born in Atlanta, Georgia, on January 15, 1929. His father was a church minister, and his family taught him to respect other people. At that time, many laws in the southern United States kept Black and white people apart. Black children were sent to different schools, and Black passengers were told to sit at the back of the bus.

In 1955, a woman named Rosa Parks was arrested in Montgomery, Alabama, because she refused to give her bus seat to a white passenger. After her arrest, a bus boycott was organized by local leaders, and King was chosen as their spokesman. For more than a year, thousands of people walked to work instead of taking the bus. Finally, the Supreme Court decided that segregation on buses was against the law.

King believed in peaceful protest. He was inspired by the ideas of Mahatma Gandhi, and he never used violence. He was arrested several times, but his message was heard by millions of people. On August 28, 1963, about 250,000 people came to the March on Washington. There, King gave his famous speech, 'I Have a Dream.' In it, he asked for a country where people are judged by their character, not by the color of their skin.

His work changed the law. In 1964, the Civil Rights Act was signed by President Lyndon Johnson. This law made it illegal to treat people unfairly because of their race at work, in schools and in public places. The same year, King was given the Nobel Peace Prize. One year later, the Voting Rights Act was passed, and many more citizens were allowed to vote.

King was killed in Memphis, Tennessee, on April 4, 1968. He was only 39 years old. Today, his birthday is celebrated every year in the United States, and his ideas are still taught in schools around the world. Many people remember him as proof that unfair laws can be changed without violence.

refusing to use or buy something as a protest

listening.title: A parking ticket
listening.intro: Listen to a police officer and a driver. Then a friend arrives. You can repeat it.

lines.text: Excuse me, sir. This car is parked in a no-parking zone.
Oh, I'm sorry, officer. I only stopped for five minutes to buy some water.
I understand, but cars are not allowed to stop here. A fine must be paid.
It is eight hundred pesos. If it is paid within ten days, you get a discount of fifty percent.
That's good. Where can I pay it?
You can pay either at any bank or online. The ticket number is written on this paper.
Thank you, officer. I'll pay it tomorrow.
Tom! What happened? Did you get a ticket?
Yes. I didn't see the sign. It was hidden behind a tree.
Rules are made for everyone's safety, you know. Next time, use the parking lot behind the market.
You're right. Parking there is cheaper, and it's safe too.
Come on, I'll buy you a coffee. Your day can only get better.
